lead: Angle modulation carries the message in the phase of a sine carrier, not in its amplitude. The envelope stays fixed, so a limiter can strip amplitude noise before detection. Phase modulation (PM) moves the phase in step with the message. Frequency modulation (FM) moves the phase in step with the integral of the message, so the instantaneous frequency follows the message itself. FM radio, TV sound, cordless phones and two-way radios use this idea. This chapter defines the two waves, their sensitivities and the modulation index, and shows how one modulator can produce the other.
prereq: You need: phasors, the Fourier transform and the complex envelope (see Hilbert transform and complex envelope).

sections.h3: Phase is the angle that moves

blocks.text: A sine carrier is s(t) = A<sub>c</sub> cos θ(t). A<sub>c</sub> is the peak amplitude in volts; θ(t) is the instantaneous phase in radians. For an unmodulated carrier θ(t) = 2πf<sub>c</sub> t, with f<sub>c</sub> in hertz, so the angle grows at 2πf<sub>c</sub> radians per second. If θ(t) is made to change in some other way, that change can carry information.

Define the instantaneous frequency f<sub>i</sub>(t) = (1/2π) dθ/dt. It is the frequency the carrier would show over a very short window, in hertz; the factor 1/2π turns radians per second into cycles per second. For the unmodulated carrier, f<sub>i</sub> = f<sub>c</sub>. In angle modulation θ(t) = 2πf<sub>c</sub> t + φ(t), where φ(t) is the excess phase in radians, so f<sub>i</sub>(t) = f<sub>c</sub> + (1/2π) dφ/dt.

There are two ways to put the message in. In PM the message sets the excess phase φ(t) itself. In FM the message sets the rate of change dφ/dt, so the instantaneous frequency follows the message and φ(t) holds the integral of the message.

As a phasor: a vector of length A<sub>c</sub> rotates at f<sub>c</sub>; modulation speeds it up and slows it down, but its tip stays on the circle of radius A<sub>c</sub>, so the envelope stays A<sub>c</sub>.
A<sub>c</sub> is the peak carrier amplitude in V; θ(t) is the instantaneous phase in rad; f<sub>i</sub>(t) is the instantaneous frequency in Hz.

sections.h3: PM and FM side by side

blocks.text: In PM the excess phase is proportional to the message: φ(t) = k<sub>p</sub> m(t), so s(t) = A<sub>c</sub> cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t + k<sub>p</sub> m(t)). k<sub>p</sub> is the phase sensitivity in radians per volt. For a tone m(t) = A<sub>m</sub> cos(2πf<sub>m</sub> t), the peak phase deviation is Δθ = k<sub>p</sub> A<sub>m</sub> radians. The frequency shifts by (1/2π) dφ/dt = −k<sub>p</sub> A<sub>m</sub> f<sub>m</sub> sin(2πf<sub>m</sub> t), so the peak frequency deviation is Δf = k<sub>p</sub> A<sub>m</sub> f<sub>m</sub>. For the same phase swing, a higher f<sub>m</sub> gives a larger frequency swing.

In FM the excess phase is proportional to the integral of the message: φ(t) = 2πk<sub>f</sub> ∫ m(τ) dτ, taken from 0 to t. k<sub>f</sub> is the frequency sensitivity in hertz per volt. For the same tone, f<sub>i</sub>(t) = f<sub>c</sub> + k<sub>f</sub> A<sub>m</sub> cos(2πf<sub>m</sub> t), so the peak deviation is Δf = k<sub>f</sub> A<sub>m</sub>. The phase term becomes (k<sub>f</sub> A<sub>m</sub>/f<sub>m</sub>) sin(2πf<sub>m</sub> t). Its peak, the modulation index β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub>, is the peak phase deviation of the FM wave in radians. For PM with a tone the equivalent index is k<sub>p</sub> A<sub>m</sub>, and it does not change when f<sub>m</sub> changes.

PM: s(t) = Ac cos(2πfc t + kp m(t))
FM: s(t) = Ac cos(2πfc t + 2πkf ∫m(τ)dτ)
k<sub>p</sub> is the phase sensitivity in rad/V; k<sub>f</sub> is the frequency sensitivity in Hz/V; m(t) is the message in V; the integral runs from 0 to t.
ΔfFM = kf Am, β = Δf/fm, ΔθPM = kp Am, ΔfPM = kp Am fm
A<sub>m</sub> is the tone peak in V; f<sub>m</sub> is the tone frequency in Hz; Δf is in Hz; β and Δθ are in rad.
Figure 3.1.1 draws worked example 1. The FM frequency swing copies the message; the PM swing copies its slope, a quarter cycle earlier.

PM and FM are close relatives. A phase modulator fed with the integral of m(t) produces FM, because its phase becomes proportional to ∫m. So an integrator followed by a phase modulator is an FM generator; this is the start of the indirect method in FM generation. A frequency modulator fed with dm/dt produces PM, because a frequency modulator's phase is the integral of its input, and the integral of dm/dt is m(t) itself. So a differentiator followed by a frequency modulator is a PM generator.
Some syllabi call k<sub>f</sub> and k<sub>p</sub> deviation constants. Keep the units straight: k<sub>f</sub> times volts gives hertz, k<sub>p</sub> times volts gives radians.

Constant envelope does not mean a narrow spectrum: a large deviation spreads the carrier into many sidebands (see Narrowband and wideband FM). The one line to remember: PM ties phase to m(t), FM ties frequency to m(t).

examples.question: A 5 kHz tone of amplitude 2 V drives an FM modulator with k<sub>f</sub> = 3 kHz/V. Find Δf and β. The same tone then drives a PM modulator with k<sub>p</sub> = 0.8 rad/V: find the peak phase deviation and the equivalent peak frequency deviation.
steps: FM: Δf = k<sub>f</sub> A<sub>m</sub> = 3 kHz/V × 2 V = 6 kHz.
β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub> = 6 kHz / 5 kHz = 1.2 (no unit; it is the peak phase swing in radians).
PM: Δθ = k<sub>p</sub> A<sub>m</sub> = 0.8 rad/V × 2 V = 1.6 rad.
Equivalent Δf for PM = Δθ × f<sub>m</sub> = 1.6 × 5000 Hz = 8000 Hz = 8 kHz.
The FM swing peaks when m(t) = +2 V; the PM swing peaks where m(t) crosses zero (Figure 3.1.1).
examples.answer: FM: Δf = 6 kHz, β = 1.2. PM: Δθ = 1.6 rad, equivalent Δf = 8 kHz.

examples.question: An angle-modulated wave is s(t) = 10 cos(2π × 10⁸ t + 5 sin 2π × 10³ t) V. Find the instantaneous frequency and its largest and smallest values, Δf, β and the power in a 1 Ω load. Then find the message m(t) if the wave is FM with k<sub>f</sub> = 2.5 kHz/V, and if it is PM with k<sub>p</sub> = 2.5 rad/V.
steps: θ(t) = 2π × 10⁸ t + 5 sin(2π × 10³ t), so f<sub>i</sub> = (1/2π) dθ/dt = 10⁸ + 5 × 10³ cos(2π × 10³ t) Hz.
f<sub>i</sub> swings between 100.005 MHz and 99.995 MHz, so Δf = 5 kHz.
f<sub>m</sub> = 1 kHz, so β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub> = 5, the same as the peak of the phase term.
Power = A<sub>c</sub>²/2 = 10²/2 = 50 W in 1 Ω. Angle modulation does not change it.
If FM: f<sub>i</sub> − f<sub>c</sub> = k<sub>f</sub> m(t), so m(t) = 5000 cos(2π × 10³ t)/2500 = 2 cos(2π × 10³ t) V.
If PM: φ(t) = k<sub>p</sub> m(t), so m(t) = 5 sin(2π × 10³ t)/2.5 = 2 sin(2π × 10³ t) V.
examples.answer: f<sub>i</sub> from 99.995 to 100.005 MHz; Δf = 5 kHz, β = 5, P = 50 W. FM message 2 cos(2π × 10³ t) V; PM message 2 sin(2π × 10³ t) V.

traps: β is not Δf. Δf = k<sub>f</sub> A<sub>m</sub> depends on the message amplitude only; β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub> also depends on the message frequency. In FM, β falls as f<sub>m</sub> rises; in PM with a tone, k<sub>p</sub> A<sub>m</sub> is fixed and the equivalent Δf rises with f<sub>m</sub>.
The FM phase carries 2πk<sub>f</sub> ∫m dt. Without the 2π the phase is in cycles, not radians, so the deviation worked out from it is 2π times too small. Keep k<sub>f</sub> in Hz/V and keep the 2π.
PM and FM both have a constant envelope, but neither has a constant instantaneous frequency. An envelope detector cannot recover the message; a frequency or phase detector is needed.
Integrator and differentiator are easy to swap: integrator then phase modulator gives FM; differentiator then frequency modulator gives PM.
A tone-modulated wave written as A<sub>c</sub> cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t + β sin 2πf<sub>m</sub> t) could be FM or PM. Find the message only from the modulator type and its constant (worked example 2).

quiz.q: Write the instantaneous frequency of an angle-modulated carrier and define each symbol.
quiz.a: f<sub>i</sub>(t) = (1/2π) dθ/dt, where θ(t) is the instantaneous phase in rad and f<sub>i</sub>(t) is the instantaneous frequency in Hz. The 1/2π turns rad/s into Hz.

quiz.q: Why does the envelope of an FM wave stay constant even though its frequency changes?
quiz.a: Modulation changes only the angle θ(t) of the carrier phasor, not its length. The tip moves on a circle of radius A<sub>c</sub>, so the envelope stays A<sub>c</sub>; only the rotation speed and the zero crossings change.

quiz.q: A 2 kHz tone of amplitude 4 V drives an FM modulator with k<sub>f</sub> = 5 kHz/V. Find Δf and β.
quiz.a: Δf = k<sub>f</sub> A<sub>m</sub> = 5 kHz/V × 4 V = 20 kHz. β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub> = 20/2 = 10.

quiz.q: For a fixed tone amplitude, compare how β changes with f<sub>m</sub> in FM and in PM.
quiz.a: FM: Δf = k<sub>f</sub> A<sub>m</sub> is fixed, so β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub> falls as 1/f<sub>m</sub>. PM: the peak phase k<sub>p</sub> A<sub>m</sub> is fixed, so the equivalent β does not change with f<sub>m</sub>, while the equivalent Δf = k<sub>p</sub> A<sub>m</sub> f<sub>m</sub> rises in proportion to f<sub>m</sub>.

quiz.q: How do you get FM from a phase modulator, and PM from a frequency modulator?
quiz.a: Put an integrator before the phase modulator: its phase then follows ∫m, which is FM. Put a differentiator before the frequency modulator: its phase is the integral of dm/dt, which is m(t) itself, so the result is PM.

beyond: Not for the exam. Angle modulation is the base of FM broadcasting and of continuous-phase digital schemes such as MSK and GMSK (GSM uses GMSK). Modern transmitters stabilise the carrier with phase-locked loops and do much of the modulation in digital signal processing. Phase noise in oscillators limits high-order QAM and radar, so it is a research topic of its own. Search next for continuous phase modulation and phase-locked loop modulators.

figure.caption: Worked example 1 drawn over two cycles of the 5 kHz tone. In FM the frequency swing copies the message, peaking at 6 kHz when m(t) is at +2 V; in PM it copies the slope of the message and peaks at 1.6 rad × 5 kHz = 8 kHz where the message crosses zero.

spec.aria: Top: a 2 volt, 5 kilohertz cosine message over 0.4 milliseconds. Bottom: the FM frequency swing, a cosine of peak 6 kilohertz, and the PM swing, a minus sine of peak 8 kilohertz.
